questions.q: Are coaching qualifications the same in all countries?

options.text: Yes, FITASC issues all of them
No, they depend on the country
There are no qualifications at all

questions.explain: Coach training and the rules for coaches differ from country to country.

questions.q: What happens if someone coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: Yellow card for the shooter; the coach is sent out
Nothing, as long as it is a coach
The shooter is given an extra target

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is not allowed in Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting.

questions.q: What comes first for a coach?

options.text: An expensive gun
The number of students
The student's safety

questions.explain: Safety comes before technique and before everything else.

questions.q: Where may you load the gun?

options.text: Anywhere at the ground, if the gun points at the ground
Only on the stand, pointing down the range, once shooting is allowed
On the way to the stand, so you are ready when called

questions.explain: Cartridges go in only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, after the referee or instructor allows shooting.

questions.q: What must you do before turning round on the stand?

options.text: Open the gun and take out all cartridges, fired or not
Put the safety catch on and keep the gun closed
Take out only the unfired cartridges, then close the gun

questions.explain: You turn round only with the gun open and empty; a safety catch is no substitute for an open gun.

questions.q: The gun clicks but does not fire. What should the shooter do?

options.text: Open it at once to see what went wrong
Turn round and show the gun to the coach
Stay put, gun down the range, and wait for the referee
Put the safety on and call for the target again

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the shooter to stay put until the referee inspects; opening or touching the safety first scores zero.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold?

options.text: One only
As many as the magazine takes
No more than two

questions.explain: In both disciplines a semi-automatic may hold no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: How is a semi-automatic carried between stands?

options.text: Closed, with the safety catch on
With the action open, muzzle up or down
On a sling over the shoulder, unloaded
With one cartridge in, safety on

questions.explain: Guns are carried open, semi-automatics with the action open, muzzles straight up or down; slings are not allowed.

questions.q: Someone shouts “Cease fire!”. What is the interpreter’s first job?

options.text: Repeat “Stop!” loudly and check that the guns are open
Explain to the guests why shooting has stopped
Ask the coach quietly what has happened
Wait until a guest asks what is going on

questions.explain: An emergency stop is repeated at once; explanations come only when all guns are open.

questions.q: Lightning is close and the referee has paused shooting. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the gun closed and wait on the stand
Open and unload the gun, then shelter in a building
Shelter under the nearest tall tree with your gun

questions.explain: During any pause the gun is open and empty, and in lightning you leave the open ground for a building.

questions.q: Where should the coach be while a child is shooting in a training session?

options.text: Behind the squad, where he can watch the whole stand
Right beside the child, able to take the gun at once
At the trap, ready to stop the targets

questions.explain: In training, direct supervision means the coach stands next to the child and can step in at once. In a competition the referee runs the stand.

questions.q: Your daughter only comes to watch a competition. Does she need hearing protection?

options.text: Yes, the rules require it near the layout
No, only the people who are shooting need it
Only if she stands right next to the stand

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for spectators near the layout; in Sporting™ children outside the clubhouse wear it at all times.

questions.q: What should you do when a child gets tired during a session?

options.text: Add one more round to build character
Switch to a harder target to keep interest
Stop the session: tiredness lowers attention

questions.explain: When attention drops the risk of a gun-handling mistake rises, so it is better to stop.

questions.q: How are guns and cartridges usually stored at home?

options.text: In the gun slip under the bed, ready for training
In a cupboard the child can open, but unloaded
In a locked safe, cartridges apart, keys with adults

questions.explain: Store guns as the law of your country requires; usually a locked safe, cartridges separately, keys only with adults.

questions.q: Why do many shooters begin with a coach rather than teach themselves?

options.text: Lessons with a coach cost less than shooting alone
A coach watches safety and catches faults before they set in
The rules do not allow shooting without a coach nearby

questions.explain: Faults are hard to feel from behind the gun, and a habit that has set in takes longer to change than to learn well from the start.

questions.q: What does a coach usually check at the first lesson?

options.text: Your ranking in national competitions
How many cartridges you can carry
Which of your eyes is the master eye

questions.explain: The master eye decides whether the gun points where you look. If your master eye is on the other side from the shoulder you shoot from (for example, left eye, right shoulder), the coach suggests a fix. Common fixes are closing one eye or putting a dot on your glasses.

questions.q: A trial lesson felt unclear and uncomfortable. What do many shooters do next?

options.text: Try a lesson with another coach
Give up clay shooting for good
Put up with it and change nothing

questions.explain: Coaches explain in different ways, and looking for one who suits you is normal.

questions.q: How many kinds of target does a beginner usually work on in the main part of a session?

options.text: All the targets the ground has
Doubles only, with no singles
One or two, shot many times

questions.explain: Many coaches find that deep work on one or two kinds of target brings a beginner more progress than single shots at many. Mixing targets comes later, once they go well.

questions.q: How do many coaches suggest approaching a double?

options.text: Break each target alone first, then both together
Shoot both targets together from the start
Practise only the second target of the pair

questions.explain: Then you already know where you will break each target of the double.

questions.q: Which targets do many coaches suggest for the end of a session?

options.text: The hardest target of the day
Targets that are already going well
A long series until you are tired

questions.explain: Ending on success builds confidence for the next session.

questions.q: Why can a lot of shots in one go hold a beginner back?

options.text: Fatigue spoils technique and repeats faults
The traps overheat and throw worse targets
The barrels wear out after fifty shots

questions.explain: Tired muscles mount the gun less precisely, and the same faults repeat.

questions.q: Which plan usually gives more progress?

options.text: A long session a few times a year
A session weekly or twice a month
Training only before competitions

questions.explain: With regular sessions the movement settles, and you lose less between sessions.

questions.q: What can happen if recoil makes your shoulder hurt?

options.text: You start to shoot more steadily
Nothing changes in your shooting
You may start to flinch at the shot

questions.explain: The body expects pain and jerks, so keep recoil under control with gun fit, a pad and cartridges with less shot.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left dominant eye. What is this called?

options.text: Central vision
Hard focus
Cross-dominance
Leading edge

questions.explain: Cross-dominance is a dominant eye on the opposite side to the shooting shoulder.

questions.q: Why is looking back at the bead to check the lead a fault?

options.text: It is forbidden by the rules of both disciplines
It usually slows or stops the gun, so the shot goes behind
The bead reflects the sun into the eye
It makes the target change colour in flight

questions.explain: When you look at the gun instead of the target, the swing tends to slow or stop. The target slips to the edge of your vision, and the shot goes behind.

questions.q: Where does the anti-dominance dot usually go?

options.text: On the safety glasses, in front of one eye
On the bead at the end of the rib
On the rib, halfway along it
On the vest line, below the shoulder

questions.explain: Safety glasses are compulsory anyway, so a small dot on the lens in front of the non-dominant eye is the simplest remedy.

questions.q: What does the hand-triangle test show?

options.text: Which eye is dominant
Whether the gun fits
How far the target flies

questions.explain: The eye that keeps the object in the triangle is the master eye.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left master eye. What is it called?

options.text: Cross-dominance
A flinch
Follow-through

questions.explain: A master eye on the other side from the stock is cross-dominance.

questions.q: Who should help you decide how to shoot with cross-dominance?

options.text: Another squad member during a competition
A qualified coach
The referee on the stand

questions.explain: A coach will take into account your age, experience and how strong the dominance is. Besides, coaching during a competition is not allowed.

questions.q: What is the length of pull?

options.text: The length of the barrels from chamber to muzzle
From the trigger to the middle of the butt pad
The height of the comb above the rib
From the rib to the bead at the muzzle

questions.explain: Length of pull is measured from the trigger to the middle of the butt pad.

questions.q: Which way is the stock bent for a right-handed shooter?

options.text: To the left (cast on)
Upwards, towards the eye
Nowhere: cast is for left-handers
To the right (cast off)

questions.explain: For right-handers it is cast off, to the right; for left-handers cast on, to the left.

questions.q: Why does gun fit matter?

options.text: Your eye is the sight, so the stock must place it right
The FITASC rules require a fitting certificate
Fit decides which gauge you may shoot
It matters for hunters only, not for clays

questions.explain: A shotgun has no rear sight: it is pointed with the eye, and a badly fitted gun keeps shooting away from where you look.

questions.q: The stock catches on clothing and lands on the arm during the mount. What is usually changed?

options.text: The length of pull: the stock is shortened
The chokes in both of the barrels
The tint of the lenses in the glasses
The shot load of the cartridges used

questions.explain: A length of pull that is too long is a common problem; the stock is shortened or a thinner pad is fitted.

questions.q: What is an adjustable comb for?

options.text: To make the gun lighter to carry
To set where the eye sits above the rib
To change the gauge of the gun
To hold spare chokes in the stock

questions.explain: Comb height decides how the eye looks along the rib.

questions.q: Do the FITASC rules allow 20-gauge guns?

options.text: No, only 12 gauge is allowed
Only for juniors under 18
Yes: the gauge may not exceed 12
Only in Compak® Sporting

questions.explain: FITASC sets an upper limit only: no larger than 12 gauge.

questions.q: Where does the coach usually want the front foot to point?

options.text: At the trap
At the pick-up point
At the referee
At the break point

questions.explain: Feet set to the break point keep the body relaxed where the shot happens. If the feet face the trap, the body cannot turn far enough to reach the break point.

questions.q: What do the Sporting™ rules require of the feet before the call?

options.text: Both feet inside the stand
The front foot on the stand line
Feet together
No requirement at all

questions.explain: The ready-position rule asks for both feet inside the 1 m shooting stand before the shooter calls.

questions.q: A left-handed shooter. The coach says “Open your front foot”. Which foot is it?

options.text: The left one, whatever the hand
The right one: a left-hander's front foot
The back foot, nearer the trap
Both feet together

questions.explain: For a left-hander the front foot is the right one. Translating “front foot” as front, not as left, avoids the mistake.

questions.q: How does a right-handed shooter usually place the feet?

options.text: Left foot slightly forward
Right foot far forward
Feet together, heels touching

questions.explain: A right-hander puts the left foot slightly forward, a left-hander the right.

questions.q: Which point should your feet be set up for?

options.text: Where the trap is
The break point
Where the squad waits

questions.explain: Then your body turns easily to exactly where you will break the target.

questions.q: Where must the shooter’s feet be in Sporting™ before calling?

options.text: Anywhere near the stand
Both inside the shooting stand
One foot inside, one outside

questions.explain: The Sporting™ rules require both feet inside the shooting stand before the call.

questions.q: In Sporting™, until when must the stock stay below the vest line?

options.text: Until the shooter has called
Until the referee gives a nod
Until the target is out and visible
Until the first shot is fired

questions.explain: The ready position is held until the target has been released and can be seen; only then may the gun be mounted.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may a shooter call for the target with the gun already at the shoulder?

options.text: No: it earns a yellow card
Only for rabbits and other low targets
Only between the two targets of a double
Yes: the gun position at the call is free

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting has no low-gun rule: the gun may be mounted or not at the call, but each target is shot from the shoulder.

questions.q: Why do coaches insist on the cheek staying on the comb?

options.text: The eye works as the rear sight, so it must sit in one place
To reduce the noise reaching the ear
Because the rules of both disciplines require it
To hide the face from the referee

questions.explain: A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job, so a lifted cheek sends the shot high.

questions.q: Which is right during the mount?

options.text: The face goes to the gun
The gun comes to the face
The head bends to the rib

questions.explain: The head stays level and the gun comes to the cheek and shoulder.

questions.q: How far below the shoulder axis is the vest line drawn in Sporting™?

options.text: 10 cm
25 cm
40 cm

questions.explain: The line is drawn 25 cm below the shoulder axis, parallel to it.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may you call for the target with the gun already mounted?

options.text: Yes, the position at the call is free
No, only from a low gun position
Only on simultaneous doubles

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free; the low gun with a vest line is a Sporting™ rule.

questions.q: Which point is about the eyes, not the gun?

options.text: Hold point
Break point
Pick-up point
Insertion point

questions.explain: The pick-up point is where the eyes first see the target clearly; the hold point is for the muzzles.

questions.q: What usually happens if the hold point is too close to the trap?

options.text: The referee calls No Bird
The gun has to chase the target
The gun has almost no room to move
The target slows down

questions.explain: Too near the trap, the target leaves at full speed past the muzzles, so the gun has to chase it. Too little room to move is the problem of a hold point too far out.

questions.q: In Sporting™, the shooter on the stand asks to see the presentation again. What is the maximum per target of the menu?

options.text: Two targets
None: no repeats are allowed
As many as the shooter wants
Exactly five

questions.explain: The referee will show it again if asked, but no more than twice per target on the menu.

questions.q: What is the hold point?

options.text: Where the barrels wait when you call
Where the cartridges are kept
Where the target lands

questions.explain: The hold point is where you hold the muzzles before calling.

questions.q: Where do your eyes go before calling?

options.text: On the barrels
To the pick-up point
On the target menu

questions.explain: Your eyes wait where the target first becomes clearly visible.

questions.q: Which point are your feet set for?

options.text: The pick-up point
The hold point
The break point

questions.explain: Feet are set for the break point, so the body is most comfortable there.

questions.q: What is perceived lead?

options.text: The real distance in front of the clay in the air
The gap the shooter sees between muzzle and target
The lead written on the target menu
The distance from the stand to the trap

questions.explain: Perceived lead is the picture at the muzzle; actual lead is the real distance in the air and is much larger.

questions.q: Of the methods with a moving gun, which usually gives the largest perceived lead?

options.text: Swing-through
Pull-away
Maintained lead
All are identical

questions.explain: With maintained lead the gun moves no faster than the target, so nothing is added on its own and you have to see the whole gap. With ambush, where the gun is still, the gap seen is even bigger.

questions.q: Which target needs almost no sideways lead?

options.text: A target going straight away
A long crosser
A quartering-away target at 45°
A crosser at 40 m

questions.explain: A straight going-away target has no sideways movement; any lead it needs is vertical.

questions.q: Why do you need lead?

options.text: So that shot and target meet
To reduce the recoil
To make the target fly slower

questions.explain: While the shot flies the target moves on, so you shoot in front of it.

questions.q: In which method do the barrels stay in front of the target throughout?

options.text: Swing-through
Maintained lead
Pull-away

questions.explain: Maintained lead: the barrels start in front and keep the gap.

questions.q: Which target needs the least lead?

options.text: A distant, fast crosser
A target going straight away
A high crossing target

questions.explain: A target going straight away or coming straight in hardly moves sideways relative to the barrels.

questions.q: With which method must the shooter see the biggest gap at the moment of decision?

options.text: Swing-through
Pull-away
Maintained lead
Ambush

questions.explain: With ambush the gun is still, and the target keeps moving during the reaction time. So the gap seen at the decision must be bigger than the actual lead.

questions.q: The coach calls: 'Behind, you stopped!' What matters most for the next shot?

options.text: The cause: the gun stopped
Only the direction 'behind'
Nothing: you saw the miss yourself
A request to add a lot more lead

questions.explain: Adding lead does not cure a stopped gun; the cause is what the shooter has to fix.

questions.q: A small but clearly visible piece breaks off the clay. The coach says 'just chipped it'. How does the referee score it?

options.text: Lost, because most of the clay flew on
No Bird
One (hit)
Hit only if the coach agrees

questions.explain: At least one visible piece makes the target a hit in both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting; the referee decides alone.

questions.q: After a hit the coach shouts 'Smoked it!'. What does he mean?

options.text: Only dust came off, so it is lost
A perfect, centred hit
It was a flash target
The shooter should change cartridges

questions.explain: In coach slang 'smoked it' is praise for a clay turned to dust, and the rules count that as a hit too. Only an intact clay that gives off a puff of dust or smoke, with no visible piece, is a zero.

questions.q: The coach says 'You lifted your head'. Where did the shot most likely go?

options.text: Behind
Over the top
Under
In front

questions.explain: Your eye does the job of a rear sight (a shotgun has none): when the head lifts, the shot usually goes over.

questions.q: A coach shouts 'Stop aiming!'. What does he want?

options.text: Don't point like a rifle: look at the target and swing
Aim more carefully along the rib at the clay
Stop shooting and open the gun at once
Lower the gun and wait for the referee

questions.explain: 'Aiming' in a coach's mouth is a fault (poking); the cure is eyes on the clay and a free swing.

questions.q: 'You rode it too long' means…

options.text: The shooter fired too early
The trap threw the target too slowly
The shooter started too far behind
The shooter followed the clay too long

questions.explain: Riding the target means following it too long, so it slows or drops and the line is lost.

questions.q: In training, a coach tells a shooter preparing for a FITASC Sporting™ competition: 'Pre-mount this one.' What is true?

options.text: Allowed in competition too, if the referee is told first
A rule change: the low gun is no longer needed in Sporting™
A training drill; in competition, mount after the target appears
A Compak® Sporting rule that applies to all FITASC disciplines

questions.explain: Sporting™ requires the gun-down ready position until the target appears; a pre-mount in competition earns a warning with a yellow card.

questions.q: 'You canted the gun' means…

options.text: The gun was tilted sideways at the shot
The gun reached the shoulder too late
The gun stopped moving at the shot
The safety catch was still on at the call

questions.explain: Canting is a sideways tilt of the gun, which pulls the shot off the line.

questions.q: Which instruction cures 'face to the gun'?

options.text: Push the head down harder
Bring the gun to your face
Close one eye
Hold the gun lower on the arm

questions.explain: The stock should come up to the face, so the eye is in the same place each time.

questions.q: What does 'eyes first, then the gun' mean on a pair?

options.text: Close the eyes after the first shot
Look at the barrel before the second shot
Mount the gun before calling for the pair
Find the second target with the eyes first

questions.explain: In a good transition the eyes lead and the gun follows.

questions.q: In a Compak® Sporting double, the shooter misses the first target and wants to fire the second cartridge at it too. Is that allowed?

options.text: Yes, the same as in Sporting™
Yes, but only on a simultaneous double
No: only one cartridge per target
Only with the referee's permission

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting forbids doubling the first target in a double; Sporting™ allows both cartridges at one target.

questions.q: In a Sporting™ double, may the shooter lower the gun between the first and the second target?

options.text: Yes, it is free between the two targets
No, the gun must stay at the shoulder
Only on a double on report
Only if the referee allows it

questions.explain: The free position applies between the targets of any double, but not before the first one.

questions.q: What must you do before practising the mount?

options.text: Load one cartridge so it feels more realistic
Nothing, as long as the gun looks empty
Open it and check the chambers are empty

questions.explain: The gun is unloaded and checked first, and no live cartridges are kept in the room.

questions.q: What decides whether you may practise the mount at home?

options.text: Your country's law on keeping and handling guns
Advice from a video you found online
Whether a friend does it at home too

questions.explain: Rules differ between countries; if in doubt, do not do it.

questions.q: In Sporting™, a shooter mounts before the call and swings along an imagined target. What follows?

options.text: Nothing, it is allowed before the call
A warning, and repeats are penalised
An extra target to shoot at

questions.explain: This is mock shooting, which the Sporting™ rules do not allow anywhere at the ground during a competition.

questions.q: What should stay the same in your routine from one target to the next?

options.text: The exact number of seconds
The order of the steps
The cartridge you load first

questions.explain: The order of the steps matters more than the seconds; the delay after the call can vary anyway (in Sporting™, and in Compak® Sporting with a manual release).

questions.q: Where is the gun when you call in Sporting™?

options.text: Already mounted firmly at the shoulder
Anywhere: the gun position is free
Down, the stock below the vest line

questions.explain: In Sporting™ the gun stays down until the target is visible. In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free.

questions.q: A noise disturbs you before you call. What can you do?

options.text: Lower the gun, breathe out and start again
Call quickly, before the same noise comes back
Ask the referee to show the target again

questions.explain: Until you call, you can restart your routine, as long as you stay within the time limit.

questions.q: Why is a pre-shot routine useful in competition?

options.text: To fill the time before the call
To bring back your usual rhythm
To show the referee you are ready

questions.explain: A familiar routine helps you keep your usual tempo and technique under pressure.

questions.q: How much time do you have between singles or between doubles in Sporting™?

options.text: At most 10 seconds
At most 30 seconds
At most 15 seconds

questions.explain: The limit in Sporting™ is 15 seconds; going over it first earns a warning.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how long do you have to call after the previous station's target?

options.text: At most 10 seconds
At most 15 seconds
As long as you need

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds; in Sporting™ the limit is 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.

questions.q: When may you load the gun?

options.text: On the way to the stand, to save time
On the stand, once the referee allows
Anywhere, as long as the safety is on

questions.explain: Load only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, once the referee has allowed shooting to start.

questions.q: What happens if someone coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: Nothing: advice from a coach is always allowed
The whole round is shot again at the end
A yellow card, and the coach is sent away

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is not allowed in either discipline: the shooter gets a yellow card and the person coaching is sent out of the shooting area.

questions.q: Which cue suits the stand?

options.text: Come on, you can do this one
Just don't miss this one again
Front edge, stay on the line

questions.explain: A short instruction about the target fits the stand; motivational phrases suit the walk between stands.

questions.q: Why can “don't” cues be risky?

options.text: They sometimes cause that very error
The referee may count them as coaching
They take too long to say on the stand

questions.explain: In studies, “don't” instructions sometimes caused the error they named, so say what to do instead.

questions.q: Where do motivational phrases fit better?

options.text: On the stand, just before the call
On the walk between stands
During the target presentation

questions.explain: In tasks that need accuracy, short instructions helped more than encouragement, so encouragement fits the time between stands.

questions.q: What is the first step of the reset after a miss?

options.text: Work out exactly why you missed
Count up your score for the round so far
Make the gun safe, as the rules say

questions.explain: Safety comes first; then one breath out, one correction, one picture and the next routine.

questions.q: When is a good time to analyse why you missed?

options.text: After the round
Before the next call
During the next presentation

questions.explain: Step-by-step analysis on the stand can disrupt your shooting; one short correction is enough there.

questions.q: You disagree with a referee's “zero”. What do you do?

options.text: Argue until the referee agrees
Protest at once, then let it go
Complain to the squad after the round

questions.explain: Protest at once in the correct way; once the decision is final, arguing on counts as an attempt to influence the referee.

questions.q: How long can a reset after a miss take?

options.text: About 5–10 seconds, inside the limit
As long as you need to feel calm again
Until the referee asks you to shoot

questions.explain: A short reset of about 5–10 seconds fits the time limits of both disciplines.

questions.q: In Sporting™, how much time do you have between singles?

options.text: At most 15 seconds
At most 60 seconds
As long as you need

questions.explain: Going over the limit earns a warning first, then penalties. In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds to call.

questions.q: In which discipline must the stock stay below the jacket line until the target appears?

options.text: In both disciplines
Only in Sporting™
Only in Compak® Sporting

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free, and there is no jacket line.

questions.q: How do studies suggest adding pressure to training?

options.text: As much as possible from the first session
Only in the week before the competition
Mild at first, then growing step by step

questions.explain: Mild pressure that grows slowly lets technique hold while you get used to it.

questions.q: May a coach advise a shooter during a competition?

options.text: Yes, but only between the stands
Yes, but only with hand signals
No: the shooter can get a yellow card

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is not allowed in either discipline, so the plan is agreed in advance.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, how long do you have to call after the previous station's target has been shot?

options.text: At most 10 seconds
At most 30 seconds
There is no limit

questions.explain: The first time you go over the limit you get a warning, written on the score sheet; if it happens again in the same round, you are penalised.

questions.q: Who should explain shooting technique to the child?

options.text: The coach, in training
Any experienced shooter nearby
The parents, during each shot

questions.explain: One voice, the coach's, does not confuse the child; the parents support.

questions.q: Which goal is a process goal?

options.text: Win the whole competition
My routine on each target
Break 25 out of 25 targets

questions.explain: A process goal is about what the child controls, not about the final score.

questions.q: May a parent give tips from behind the stand during a competition?

options.text: Yes, if they speak quietly
Yes, between two targets
No, it counts as coaching

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition can earn the child a yellow card, and the person coaching is sent away.

questions.q: What can a parent do right after a bad round?

options.text: Explain all the mistakes at once, in detail
Let the child start the talk later
Compare the score with the other children

questions.explain: Give the child time to cool down; going over the round is the coach's job when the child is ready.

questions.q: A coach and a shooter share no language. What helps most in the first session?

options.text: Long explanations, spoken slowly
Shooting more targets in silence
Agreed anchor words and hand signals
A translation app during the routine

questions.explain: A small agreed vocabulary and the coach’s signals carry most of a session; long explanations and phones during the routine get in the way.

questions.q: At a competition, the shooter’s coach asks the interpreter to pass on a tip. What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly between targets
Pass it on with the referee’s nod
Pass it on only between stands
Decline: pass on only official words

questions.explain: Coaching during the competition is forbidden, and the rules do not mention interpreters. Passing on only the referee, the jury and the organiser protects the shooter.

questions.q: When should the coach and the interpreter talk to the shooter on the stand?

options.text: While the shooter mounts
Just before the call
During the swing
When the gun is open

questions.explain: The shooter’s routine ends with the shot, and by the time the gun is closed it is well under way; words during it break the shooter’s focus.
